prompt: A security team assigns its backlog of 300 old scanner findings to the developers and calls it shifting left. What is missing for it to be a shift left in the lesson's sense?

choices.text: A larger security team to support the developers through the backlog
choices.why: Headcount is not the point; the findings would still arrive long after the changes that caused them.

choices.text: Findings about the change its author is working on
choices.why: Right. Shifting left moves the feedback earlier in a change's life; this moved a queue to another desk.

choices.text: A scanner that runs in the editor instead of the pipeline
choices.why: Moving the scanner earlier still leaves 300 findings about code nobody is changing.

choices.text: Training the developers in secure coding first
choices.why: Training helps, but the queue would still be about old code and not about the change in front of them.

prompt: Why can an image scan not be moved into the editor?

choices.text: It is too slow for anything but the nightly run
choices.why: Lesson 8 runs it on every push, so speed is not what keeps it out of the editor.

choices.text: Editors do not run security tools
choices.why: Editors run linters and Semgrep rules; the limit is what exists to be read.

choices.text: There is no image while the code is being typed
choices.why: Right. A check moves only as far left as the thing it reads exists.

choices.text: Scanning images needs administrator rights on the laptop
choices.why: It needs access to Docker, which the pipeline's machine has too; that is not the reason.

prompt: linkbox's code has not changed in a year, and this morning an advisory is published for a library it uses. Which place on the line can notice?

choices.text: The pre-commit hook, on the next commit anybody makes
choices.why: There may be no next commit for months; the hook only runs when somebody commits.

choices.text: The push pipeline, which re-reads every dependency
choices.why: It re-reads them only when somebody pushes, and nobody is pushing.

choices.text: None until a developer changes the code
choices.why: That is the misuse the lesson names: leaving the right-hand end of the line empty.

choices.text: The checks that watch what is already running
choices.why: Right. No check on the left can see it, because the change it would run on does not exist.

prompt: What does the lesson say about the "100 times after release" figure attributed to the IBM Systems Sciences Institute?

choices.text: It was measured on large waterfall projects in the 1970s
choices.why: That describes Boehm's data, which is a different source; the IBM chart has no study anybody has found.

choices.text: No study with data behind it has been found
choices.why: Right. The trail ends at course notes cited second hand.

choices.text: It is accurate for security findings but not for bugs
choices.why: Nobody measured security findings in a pipeline either; the lesson gives it no domain where it holds.

choices.text: It was withdrawn by IBM in a later correction
choices.why: There is no correction to withdraw, because there is no published study.

prompt: Boehm and Basili's 2001 list gave a large ratio for late defects. What did the same item say about small, non-critical systems?

choices.text: That the ratio was closer to 5 to 1
choices.why: Right. The large ratio was for large projects with long phases.

choices.text: That the ratio was the same, 100 to 1
choices.why: The item separated the two cases precisely because the ratio was not the same.

choices.text: That small systems had no measurable difference
choices.why: There was a difference; it was much smaller.

choices.text: That they had not been studied at all
choices.why: They were in the item, with their own ratio.

prompt: Which of these are reasons the lesson gives for a late finding costing more, without needing a multiplier? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The author has lost the context of the change
choices.why: Right: a week later they read the code like anybody else.

choices.text: Other code has been built on top of the flawed change
choices.why: Right: the fix then touches more than the line that was wrong.

choices.text: Copies of the artefact are in the registry and on servers
choices.why: Right: every copy has to be reached by the fix.

choices.text: Scanners report fewer findings on older code
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; a scanner reads old code the same way as new.

prompt: What budget does the lesson give the checks that run on every push, and where does the number come from?

choices.text: About ten minutes, from XP's ten-minute build practice
choices.why: Right. It is about how long a person waits before switching to another task.

choices.text: About an hour, because the push runs on a server
choices.why: An hour is the nightly run's budget, where nobody waits.

choices.text: Under a second, so it never interrupts anybody
choices.why: That is the editor's budget; a build alone takes longer than a second.

choices.text: A few seconds, as measured on linkbox
choices.why: linkbox's push is fast today, but the budget is set by people's patience, not by one service's timings.

prompt: Lesson 6 puts a secret scan in the pre-commit hook. Why does it also run as the first stage of every push?

choices.text: The hook only reads the staged lines, so it cannot find anything
choices.why: It finds secrets in the staged lines, which is its job; the reason for the second run is that the hook can be skipped.

choices.text: Running the same check twice halves its false positives
choices.why: Running it twice changes nothing about its accuracy.

choices.text: A hook lives in one clone, and --no-verify skips it
choices.why: Right. A check that matters is never only on the laptop.

choices.text: The server's copy of gitleaks is newer
choices.why: Both run the same version; the difference is who controls whether it runs.

prompt: Match each check to the place the lesson gives it.

pairs.left: a scan of the staged lines for secrets
tests, static analysis and the build
a rebuild with no cache and the dynamic scan
new advisories about what is already deployed

prompt: A new check reads the whole repository and takes 3 minutes today; the repository grows 40% a year. It fits the push budget now. What does the lesson suggest watching?

choices.text: Nothing: a check that fits the budget stays where it is
choices.why: That is how budgets are lost quietly: each check fits when it is added, and the code grows under all of them.

choices.text: Its time on every run, because it grows with the code
choices.why: Right. The second kind of check, reading a lot, is where budgets are lost one second at a time.

choices.text: Its findings count, which decides where it belongs
choices.why: Where a check belongs depends on its cost and what it reads, not on how much it finds.

choices.text: Whether the editor can run it instead
choices.why: Something that reads the whole repository for minutes is the opposite of what fits the editor.

prompt: Run on the laptop, ci/pipeline.sh failed in the test stage while the same commit passes on the server. Why?

choices.text: The laptop has a different version of uv
choices.why: Both use the same uv; the message was about a directory that already existed.

choices.text: The tests depend on the server's database
choices.why: Each test makes its own database in a temporary directory; nothing came from the server.

choices.text: The .venv from lesson 1 was still there
choices.why: Right. The hook clones into an empty directory, so the laptop's state is what differs.

choices.text: CI_COMMIT was not set on the laptop
choices.why: Only the build uses CI_COMMIT, and without it the tag is dev; the test stage failed first.

prompt: You run the pipeline from a fresh clone of your project. What does that run not test?

choices.text: The image build, which needs CI_COMMIT
choices.why: The clone's pipeline builds the image like the server's, tagged dev.

choices.text: Changes you have not committed yet
choices.why: Right. A clone carries commits; for uncommitted work, run the one fast tool directly.

choices.text: The tests, which need the server's database
choices.why: The tests ran and passed in the clone.

choices.text: The pinned dependencies
choices.why: The test stage installs them from requirements.txt in the clone, as on the server.

prompt: The runner without the guard line was given a list name with a typo. What exit status did it return?
Why does the lesson treat a missing list as a failure rather than as an empty pipeline that passes?

choices.text: Because bash cannot read a missing file
choices.why: bash reads nothing and carries on, which is exactly the problem: it reached "pipeline passed".

choices.text: Because a pass with nothing run looks like a real pass
choices.why: Right. In a scheduled job nobody watches, it would report a pass every night.

choices.text: Because an empty list is a syntax error in ci/stages
choices.why: An empty list is a valid file with no stages; the case here is a file that is not there.

choices.text: Because the hook would refuse the push if the list were missing
choices.why: The hook runs whatever the pipeline answers; it refuses nothing on its own.

prompt: Timing the pieces of the test stage in the clean clone, which piece took most of the time?

choices.text: Making the virtual environment
choices.why: It took 0.028 seconds.

choices.text: Installing the packages
choices.why: It took 0.073 seconds, because uv linked them from its cache.

choices.text: Running pytest
choices.why: Right: 1.062 seconds real, of which the tests themselves were 0.43.

choices.text: Cloning the repository
choices.why: The clone was not timed on its own, and it is not part of the test stage.

prompt: On a hosted runner that starts every job from an empty machine, which piece of the test stage grows the most compared with the recording?

choices.text: The install, with no cache
choices.why: Right. The 0.073 seconds came from the cache in ~/.cache/uv; an empty machine downloads every package.

choices.text: pytest, because the runner's processors are slower
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says hosted processors are slower; the cache is the difference it names.

choices.text: Making the environment, which needs a download of Python
choices.why: The lesson measured it at 0.028 seconds and named no download for it.

choices.text: None: the stage is the same script
choices.why: The same script on a machine with nothing cached does more work.

prompt: The pipeline prints "build: passed in 0s". What does that mean?

choices.text: The build was skipped
choices.why: It ran and passed; the 0 is a measurement.

choices.text: It took less than about a second
choices.why: Right. SECONDS counts whole seconds, so a reading is up to a second off either way.

choices.text: The clock was not started
choices.why: start is set from SECONDS before every stage.

choices.text: Docker reused another machine's image
choices.why: It reused layers on the same machine, which is why it was fast.

prompt: What can the nightly rebuild with --no-cache find that the cached build on every push cannot?

choices.text: A newer python:3.13 published on Docker Hub since the last build
choices.why: The rebuild uses the base image already on the machine; picking up a newer one takes docker pull or --pull.

choices.text: A vulnerability in the image
choices.why: It does not scan what it built; lesson 8's image scan reads the result.

choices.text: A build that only works because of what is cached
choices.why: Right. Every step runs again, so a package withdrawn from the index shows up on an ordinary night.

choices.text: A failing test
choices.why: The rebuild runs no tests; ci/stages, which runs first, does.

prompt: Why does the by-hand nightly run start with ci/pipeline.sh and only then run ci/pipeline.sh ci/nightly?

choices.text: Because ci/nightly cannot be read before ci/stages
choices.why: Each list is read on its own; the order is a decision about which main gets the slow checks.

choices.text: So the slow checks run only on a main whose push checks passed
choices.why: Right. ci/nightly's own comment says it runs after everything in ci/stages has passed.

choices.text: So that the rebuild can reuse the cache the first run left behind
choices.why: The rebuild uses --no-cache, so nothing the first run made is reused.

choices.text: Because cron can only start one command
choices.why: The crontab line chains both with &&; cron is not the reason.

prompt: Cron starts commands with a minimal ___, so a crontab that runs linkbox's tests has to set it to include ~/.local/bin, where uv lives.
Put the places a check can run in order along the line, from left to right.
A team's push pipeline has grown to 25 minutes and developers have started batching changes. The slowest stage is a dynamic scan of a staging copy. What does the lesson's model suggest?

choices.text: Mark the dynamic scan as allowed to fail
choices.why: It would still cost 25 minutes and its findings would stop being read: lesson 1's end of the road.

choices.text: Delete the dynamic scan, since static analysis already covers what it finds
choices.why: Static analysis cannot see responses, which is what a dynamic scan reads.

choices.text: Run it in the editor so developers see it first
choices.why: There is no running staging copy while somebody types.

choices.text: Move it to the nightly list, and send its result to a person in the morning
choices.why: Right. It still runs every day on main, and nobody's push waits for it.

prompt: A slide quotes a 100x cost multiplier to justify adding a scanner to the push pipeline. What would the lesson have you say instead?

choices.text: The checkable reasons, and what your pipeline measured
choices.why: Right. Context, code built on top, copies and exposure, plus your own minutes from push to result.

choices.text: A larger multiplier from a more recent study
choices.why: The lesson names no such study, and swapping one unsourced number for another spends the same trust.

choices.text: The same figure, with Boehm cited as its source
choices.why: Boehm's data is a different source, from large projects, and the same paper gave about 5 to 1 for small systems.

choices.text: Nothing: developers accept checks without reasons
choices.why: The lesson argues the opposite: the programme runs on being believed.
